qs.ex: Under Rule 112, Sec. 3(d), if the respondent cannot be subpoenaed, or if subpoenaed does not submit counter-affidavits within the 10-day period, the investigating officer shall resolve the complaint based on the evidence presented by the complainant.
qs.key: Resolve based on complainant's evidence
qs.lb: Rule 112, Sec. 3(d), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: The investigating prosecutor finds prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction and files the information without the city prosecutor's prior written approval.
o: None, since any investigating fiscal may file
Lack of prior written authority, waivable
The charge is void and cannot be cured
The court must dismiss it motu proprio
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4; Rule 117, Sec. 3(d). Under Villa Gomez v. People (2020, En Banc), lack of the head prosecutor's prior written authority is a ground to quash that is waived if not raised before plea. Under DOJ DC No. 015 (2024) (upheld in Meking v. Remulla, 2025), NPS prosecutors apply PFC + RCC.
qs.key: Lack of prior written authority, waivable
qs.lb: Rule 112, Sec. 4 & Rule 117, Secs. 3(d) & 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Villa Gomez v. People (G.R. No. 216824, Nov. 10, 2020, En Banc); DOJ DC No. 015 (2024); Meking v. Remulla (G.R. No. 280455, Nov. 11, 2025, En Banc)

qs.tw: The information is properly filed. Within 10 days, the RTC judge reads only the prosecutor's certification and issues a warrant.
o: Yes, the sworn certification is sufficient
No, the judge must evaluate the records
Yes, the prosecutor already screened it
No, the judge must hold a witness hearing
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a): the judge must personally evaluate the prosecutor's resolution and supporting evidence to determine judicial probable cause. Personal examination of witnesses is optional, but relying on the certification alone is improper.
qs.key: No, the judge must evaluate the records
qs.lb: Art. III, Sec. 2, 1987 Constitution; Rule 112, Sec. 5(a), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Soliven v. Makasiar (G.R. No. 82585, 1988); Lim v. Felix (G.R. Nos. 94054–57, 1991)

qs.tw: The judge has doubts about probable cause.
o: Dismiss the criminal case right away
Order additional evidence within 5 days
Conduct a new preliminary investigation
Refer the records back to the DOJ
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a): in case of doubt regarding judicial probable cause, the judge may order the prosecutor to present additional evidence within 5 days and must resolve the issue within 30 days from filing.
qs.key: Order additional evidence within 5 days
qs.lb: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Instead, the evidence clearly fails to show probable cause.
o: Issue the arrest warrant anyway
Immediately dismiss the case
Return the records to the fiscal
Wait for a defense motion first
qs.ex: Under Rule 112, Sec. 5(a), the judge shall not issue a warrant of arrest if the accused is already under detention pursuant to a warrant issued by the MTC or lawfully arrested without a warrant, or if the offense is punishable by fine only (in which case a commitment order or summons issues instead).
qs.key: Immediately dismiss the case
qs.lb: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a), 2nd sent., Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Rewind: the city prosecutor dismissed Uma's complaint. Uma petitions the Secretary of Justice, who reverses.
o: No, the city prosecutor's ruling is final
Yes, the Secretary may reverse or modify
Only if the trial court approves it first
Only if the respondent consents to review
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4; DOJ DC No. 015 (2024): on petition for review, the Secretary of Justice may reverse or modify the prosecutor's resolution and direct the filing of an information.
qs.key: Yes, the Secretary may reverse or modify
qs.lb: Rule 112, Sec. 4, last par., Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; DOJ DC No. 015 (2024); Ledesma v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 113216, 1997)

S.title: Hot pursuit, methods, and escapes
S.base: Police arrive at a market ten minutes after a stabbing. They see the victim, hear eyewitnesses describe a man in a green shirt who just ran off, and find a man in a blood-stained green shirt nearby.

qs.q: Can they arrest him without a warrant?
o: No, because they did not see the stabbing
Yes, under a valid hot pursuit arrest
Only if the suspect confesses on the spot
Only with a barangay official present
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b): hot pursuit — offense just committed, plus probable cause based on personal knowledge of facts and circumstances.
qs.key: Yes, under a valid hot pursuit arrest
qs.lb: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Pestilos v. Generoso (G.R. No. 182601, Nov. 10, 2014)

qs.tw: Instead, police arrest him three days later, based only on a witness's statement.
o: Yes, as a valid hot pursuit arrest
No, it lacks immediacy and own knowledge
Yes, because an eyewitness identified him
Yes, if arrested within seven days
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b): hot pursuit requires immediacy (offense "just committed") and probable cause based on personal knowledge; after three days, police need a warrant.
qs.key: No, it lacks immediacy and own knowledge
qs.lb: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Go v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101837, 1992); People v. Del Rosario (G.R. No. 127755, 1999)

qs.tw: Police get a warrant. The arresting officer does not have it with him. The suspect demands to see it.
o: No, the officer must hold it in hand
Yes, if shown as soon as practicable
Only if the suspect consents to arrest
No, the suspect may lawfully refuse
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 7: the arresting officer need not have the warrant in his possession at the time of arrest, but must show it as soon as practicable afterward if required.
qs.key: Yes, if shown as soon as practicable
qs.lb: Rule 113, Sec. 7, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Mallari v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 110569, 1996)

qs.tw: The suspect runs into his house and refuses to open the door.
o: Wait outside and secure a search warrant
Break in after notice and refused entry
Do nothing, as private homes are inviolable
Merely notify the suspect's legal counsel
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 11: the officer may break into any building or enclosure after announcing his authority and purpose and being refused admittance.
qs.key: Break in after notice and refused entry
qs.lb: Rule 113, Sec. 11, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Different scene: a private citizen sees a man snatch a bag and grabs him.
o: No, only peace officers may effect arrests
Yes, a valid warrantless citizen's arrest
Only when a barangay official is present
Only if the arresting citizen is a lawyer
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5: a private person may arrest without a warrant in the same situations (in flagrante, hot pursuit, escapee) and must deliver the person to the nearest police station or jail.
qs.key: Yes, a valid warrantless citizen's arrest
qs.lb: Rule 113, Secs. 5 & 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Citizen's Arrest

qs.tw: The arrested man escapes from jail a week later.
qs.q: Do police need a warrant to recapture him?
o: Yes, police must first secure a new warrant
No, an escapee may be retaken anywhere
Only if caught within the same city
Only if recaptured within 24 hours
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 13: an escaped person may be immediately pursued and retaken without a warrant at any time and anywhere in the Philippines.
qs.key: No, an escapee may be retaken anywhere
qs.lb: Rule 113, Secs. 5(c) & 13, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Parulan v. Director of Prisons (G.R. No. L-28519, 1968)

S.title: Bail: how it works day to day
S.base: Wena is charged with estafa (bailable as a matter of right). She is out on a property bond.

qs.q: Until when does her bail stay in force?
o: Only until her formal arraignment
Until promulgation of the RTC judgment
Only until the prosecution rests its case
Until the case reaches the Supreme Court
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(a): bail remains effective at all stages of the case until promulgation of the judgment of the RTC, unless cancelled earlier.
qs.key: Until promulgation of the RTC judgment
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 2(a), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Maguddatu v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 139599, 2000)

qs.tw: Wena, already arraigned, skips a trial date without justification despite notice.
o: Trial must be postponed until she appears
Trial may validly proceed in absentia
The criminal case is outright dismissed
She is automatically declared convicted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(c); Rule 115, Sec. 1(c). Trial in absentia needs arraignment, notice, and unjustified absence.
qs.key: Trial may validly proceed in absentia
qs.lb: Art. III, Sec. 14(2), 1987 Constitution; Rule 114, Sec. 2(c) & Rule 115, Sec. 1(c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Gimenez v. Nazareno (G.R. No. L-37933, 1988)

qs.tw: The court declares her bond forfeited.
o: Pay the full bond amount immediately
Produce her and explain within 30 days
Nothing, as forfeiture is already final
Simply file an application for new bail
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 21: bondsmen have 30 days to produce the accused and explain why judgment should not be rendered against them; if they fail, judgment issues jointly and severally.
qs.key: Produce her and explain within 30 days
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 21, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Reliance Surety & Insurance Co. v. Amante, Jr. (G.R. No. 150994, 2005)

qs.tw: Wena is acquitted.
o: The bondsmen must apply to cancel it
It is automatically cancelled
It stays active pending any appeal
It is forfeited in favor of the State
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 22: automatically cancelled on acquittal, dismissal, or execution of a judgment of conviction.
qs.key: It is automatically cancelled
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 22, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Rewind: Wena could not post bail and has been detained for as long as the maximum imprisonment for the offense.
o: She stays detained until final judgment
She is released while trial continues
She must still post a reduced cash bail
She is automatically deemed acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 16: an accused detained for a period equal to or more than the possible maximum imprisonment shall be released immediately, without prejudice to continuation of the trial.
qs.key: She is released while trial continues
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 16, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; R.A. No. 10592

qs.tw: Out on bail, Wena tries to fly abroad without the court's permission.
qs.q: Can she be arrested without a warrant?
o: No, because she is currently out on bail
Yes, leaving without permission allows it
Only by her bondsman, not police officers
Only after the court cancels her bond
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 23: an accused released on bail may be re-arrested without a warrant if she attempts to depart from the Philippines without permission of the court.
qs.key: Yes, leaving without permission allows it
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 23, par. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Manotoc, Jr. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. L-62100, 1986)

qs.tw: Before arraignment, Wena (out on bail) moves to quash the warrant for lack of probable cause.
o: Yes, posting bail waives all objections
No, if raised before entering a plea
Yes, unless she posted a cash bond
Only if the public prosecutor objects
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 26: applying for or posting bail does not bar challenges to the validity of arrest, the warrant, or preliminary investigation, provided raised before entering a plea.
qs.key: No, if raised before entering a plea
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 26, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Okabe v. Gutierrez (G.R. No. 150185, 2004)

qs.tw: New accused: Xyla, still at large and not arrested, files a petition for bail.
o: Yes, because bail is a matter of right
No, she must be in custody of the law
Yes, if she posts double the bond amount
Only if charged with a light offense
qs.ex: Jurisprudence (e.g., Paderanga v. CA): only a person in custody, by arrest or voluntary surrender, may apply for bail.
qs.key: No, she must be in custody of the law
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 1, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Miranda v. Tuliao (G.R. No. 158763, Mar. 31, 2006); Paderanga v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 115407, 1995)

S.title: Pleas, plea bargaining, and pre-trial
S.base: Yuri is charged with murder. At arraignment, the victim's family (the offended party) and the prosecutor are present.

qs.q: Yuri offers to plead guilty to homicide. What is needed?
o: Only the trial court judge's express approval
Consent of offended party and prosecutor
Only the public prosecutor's consent
An amended information for homicide
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2: a plea to a lesser offense necessarily included in the charge requires consent of the offended party and the prosecutor, plus court approval. No amendment is needed.
qs.key: Consent of offended party and prosecutor
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Daan v. Sandiganbayan (G.R. Nos. 163972–77, 2008)

qs.tw: The offended party does not appear at arraignment despite due notice.
qs.q: Can the plea to homicide still be accepted?
o: No, the offended party must always consent
Yes, with the prosecutor's consent alone
Only after postponing the arraignment once
Only if Yuri pays civil damages up front
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(f): if the offended party fails to appear at arraignment despite due notice, the court may allow the plea with the conformity of the trial prosecutor alone.
qs.key: Yes, with the prosecutor's consent alone
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 1(f), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded not guilty at arraignment. Before trial, he wants to plead guilty to homicide.
o: Yes, no plea change is allowed afterward
No, he may withdraw it before trial
Only after filing a new information
Only once the trial has already begun
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2: after arraignment but before trial, the accused may still withdraw his not-guilty plea and plead guilty to the lesser included offense with the required consents.
qs.key: No, he may withdraw it before trial
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 2, 2nd sent., Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded guilty to homicide. Before the judgment becomes final, he says he did not understand the plea.
o: No, a guilty plea is immediately final
Yes, anytime before judgment is final
Only if moved prior to his sentencing
Only by raising it on ordinary appeal
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 5: at any time before the judgment of conviction becomes final, the court may permit an improvident plea of guilty to be withdrawn and replaced with a not-guilty plea.
qs.key: Yes, anytime before judgment is final
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 5, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; People v. Villarama, Jr. (G.R. No. 99287, 1992)

qs.tw: Rewind: the information is vague about how Yuri took part. Before arraignment, he asks for a bill of particulars.
o: No, bills of particulars are civil only
Yes, if it specifies defects before plea
Only after the prosecution rests its case
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 9: the accused may move for a bill of particulars before arraignment, specifying the alleged defects and the details desired.
qs.key: Yes, if it specifies defects before plea
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Enrile v. People (G.R. No. 213455, Aug. 11, 2015, En Banc)

qs.tw: At arraignment, Yuri appears unable to understand the charge because of an unsound mental condition.
o: Enter a plea of not guilty for him
Suspend arraignment for mental exam
Proceed, since defense counsel is there
Dismiss the criminal case outright
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 11(a): arraignment is suspended when the accused appears to suffer from an unsound mental condition rendering him unable to understand the charge, and the court orders a mental examination.
qs.key: Suspend arraignment for mental exam
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 11(a), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Yuri stays outside the courtroom, and his lawyer enters a plea of not guilty for him.
o: Yes, defense counsel may plead for him
No, the accused must plead personally
Yes, if duly entered in court records
Yes, for pleas of not guilty only
qs.ex: Under Rule 116, Sec. 1(b) of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure, the accused must be personally present at the arraignment and must personally enter his or her plea of guilty or not guilty.
qs.key: No, the accused must plead personally
qs.lb: Rule 116, Sec. 1(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: At pre-trial, Yuri's lawyer signs a written stipulation admitting Yuri was at the scene. Yuri does not sign it.
qs.q: Can the stipulation be used against Yuri?
o: Yes, counsel's signature binds the client
No, both accused and counsel must sign
Yes, if approved by the trial court
Only as to the civil liability aspect
qs.ex: Rule 118, Sec. 2: all agreements or admissions made at pre-trial must be reduced to writing and signed by both the accused and counsel; otherwise they cannot be used against the accused.
qs.key: No, both accused and counsel must sign
qs.lb: Rule 118, Sec. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Fule v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 79094, June 22, 1988)

S.title: More quash grounds and jeopardy exceptions
S.base: Zed is charged with a light offense. The information was filed after the offense had already prescribed.

o: The facts charged fail to constitute an offense
Criminal action or liability is extinguished
The court has no jurisdiction over his person
The information does not conform to prescribed form
qs.ex: Under Rule 117, Sec. 3(g) and Art. 89(5) of the RPC, the accused may move to quash the complaint or information on the ground that the criminal action or liability has been extinguished by prescription.
qs.key: Criminal action or liability is extinguished
qs.lb: Rule 117, Sec. 3(g), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Art. 89(5), Revised Penal Code

qs.tw: Zed raises prescription only on appeal, after conviction.
o: Yes, all grounds must be raised before plea
No, extinction of liability is never waived
Yes, unless the prosecution expressly agrees
Only with respect to the civil aspect
qs.ex: Under Rule 117, Sec. 9, extinction of the criminal action or liability (such as prescription under Sec. 3[g]) is one of the four non-waivable grounds that survive arraignment and plea and may be raised at any stage of the proceedings.
qs.key: No, extinction of liability is never waived
qs.lb: Rule 117, Secs. 3(g) & 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Cabral v. Puno (G.R. No. L-41692, 1976)

qs.tw: New case: an MTC tries Zed for an offense that belongs to the RTC. He is arraigned and convicted. The case is then refiled in the RTC.
qs.q: Is the RTC case barred by double jeopardy?
o: Yes, because he was already convicted once
No, the first court lacked jurisdiction
Yes, because he was formally arraigned
No, but he gets credit for time served
qs.ex: First jeopardy needs a court of competent jurisdiction (Rule 117, Sec. 7). Lack of jurisdiction over the offense is never waived.
qs.key: No, the first court lacked jurisdiction
qs.lb: Art. III, Sec. 21, 1987 Constitution; Rule 117, Secs. 3(b), 7 & 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Zed was never validly arrested, but he posted bail, was arraigned, and only then moved to quash for lack of jurisdiction over his person.
o: Yes, personal jurisdiction is never waived
No, it was waived by entering a plea
Yes, because his warrantless arrest failed
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Lack of jurisdiction over the person is waivable (it is not among a, b, g, i). Objections must be raised before plea (Rule 114, Sec. 26; Rule 117, Sec. 9).
qs.key: No, it was waived by entering a plea
qs.lb: Rule 114, Sec. 26 & Rule 117, Secs. 3(c) & 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Miranda v. Tuliao (G.R. No. 158763, 2006)

qs.tw: Zed was convicted of slight physical injuries after pleading guilty to that lesser offense without the prosecutor's or offended party's consent. He is now charged with serious physical injuries for the same act.
o: Yes, double jeopardy bars the graver case
No, his unconsented plea does not bar it
Yes, unless new evidence later surfaced
No, provided the accused consents to it
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(c): a plea of guilty to a lesser offense without the consent of the prosecutor and offended party does not bar prosecution for the graver offense. Credit for time served applies.
qs.key: No, his unconsented plea does not bar it
qs.lb: Rule 117, Sec. 7(c) & Rule 116, Sec. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; People v. Villarama, Jr. (G.R. No. 99287, 1992)

qs.tw: Instead, the facts making up the graver offense existed at the time of his plea but were discovered only afterward.
o: Yes, because those facts already existed
No, facts discovered later permit it
Yes, unless the accused gives consent
Only if the victim subsequently died
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(b): conviction does not bar prosecution for a graver offense when the facts constituting it were discovered only after the filing of the former complaint or information / plea.
qs.key: No, facts discovered later permit it
qs.lb: Rule 117, Sec. 7(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Different information: its own allegations show that Zed acted in lawful self-defense.
o: The facts do not constitute an offense
Averments show a legal justification
The court lacks territorial jurisdiction
The charge violates double jeopardy
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(h): the complaint or information contains averments which, if true, would constitute a legal excuse or justification.
qs.key: Averments show a legal justification
qs.lb: Rule 117, Sec. 3(h), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

S.title: Trial procedure and witnesses
S.base: Abel is on trial for homicide.

qs.q: Abel admits killing the victim but claims self-defense. Can the order of trial change?
o: No, the prosecution always presents first
Yes, the court may order a reverse trial
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
No, reverse trial exists only in civil law
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 11(e): when the accused admits the act or omission charged in the complaint or information but interposes a lawful defense, the order of trial may be modified (reverse trial).
qs.key: Yes, the court may order a reverse trial
qs.lb: Rule 119, Sec. 11(e), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: A key prosecution witness is about to leave the Philippines with no definite date of return.
qs.q: How can the testimony be preserved?
o: It cannot; trial must wait for his return
Conditional exam before the trial court
By submitting a sworn judicial affidavit
By deposition before a notary abroad
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 15: a prosecution witness who is too sick or about to leave the Philippines may be conditionally examined before the court where the case is pending, with the accused present or notified.
qs.key: Conditional exam before the trial court
qs.lb: Rule 119, Sec. 15, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Vda. de Manguerra v. Risos (G.R. No. 152643, Aug. 28, 2008); Go v. People (G.R. No. 185527, July 18, 2012)

qs.tw: Instead, a defense witness is sick and lives more than 100 km away with no means to travel.
qs.q: Before whom may the witness be conditionally examined?
o: Only before the trial court trying the case
A judge, designated lawyer, or MTC judge
Any commissioned notary public nearby
The public prosecutor handling the case
qs.ex: Rule 119, Secs. 12–13: a defense witness may be conditionally examined before a judge, a member of the bar in good standing designated by the judge, or an inferior court judge.
qs.key: A judge, designated lawyer, or MTC judge
qs.lb: Rule 119, Secs. 12–13, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: A witness testified in an earlier case with the same parties and subject matter, where Abel cross-examined him. The witness has since died.
qs.q: Can that earlier testimony be used against Abel?
o: No, it violates his right to confrontation
Yes, prior cross-examined testimony applies
Only if Abel expressly consents to its use
Yes, solely as to the civil liability aspect
qs.ex: Rule 115, Sec. 1(f): prior testimony of a dead or unavailable witness given in another proceeding with the same parties and subject matter is admissible where the adverse party had the opportunity to cross-examine.
qs.key: Yes, prior cross-examined testimony applies
qs.lb: Rule 115, Sec. 1(f), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Rule 130, Sec. 49, Revised Rules on Evidence

qs.tw: Before he was ever arraigned, a co-accused, Bart, escaped.
qs.q: Can Bart be tried in absentia?
o: Yes, fugitives may be tried in absentia
No, trial in absentia needs arraignment
Yes, once defense counsel is appointed
Yes, after thirty days of non-appearance
qs.ex: Constitution and Rule 115, Sec. 1(c): requisites are arraignment, due notice, and unjustified absence.
qs.key: No, trial in absentia needs arraignment
qs.lb: Art. III, Sec. 14(2), 1987 Constitution; Rule 115, Sec. 1(c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Gimenez v. Nazareno (1988)

qs.tw: Trial has gone on for over 180 days because of prosecution delays. Abel never moved to dismiss before trial. Now, after trial, he moves to dismiss for violation of speedy trial.
qs.q: Will the motion prosper under Rule 119?
o: Yes, the 180-day limit was clearly violated
No, failure to move before trial waived it
Yes, dismissal becomes automatic after 180 days
Only if the public prosecutor consents
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 9: failure of the accused to move for dismissal prior to trial constitutes a waiver of the right to dismissal under the statutory speedy-trial rule. The constitutional right remains separate (Sec. 10).
qs.key: No, failure to move before trial waived it
qs.lb: Rule 119, Secs. 9–10, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; R.A. No. 8493 (Speedy Trial Act of 1998)

qs.tw: Different case: Cora is charged with estafa, but the evidence shows only theft, which is not included in estafa. Judgment has not yet been rendered.
o: Acquit and release Cora right away
Commit her for the proper new charge
Convict Cora of the offense of theft
Convict Cora of estafa as charged
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 19: if it appears before judgment that a mistake was made in charging the proper offense, the court shall not discharge the accused if there is good cause to detain, commit her to answer for the proper offense, and dismiss the original case upon filing of the proper information.
qs.key: Commit her for the proper new charge
qs.lb: Rule 119, Sec. 19 & Rule 110, Sec. 14, par. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Back to Abel. After both sides rest but before judgment, a new witness surfaces.
qs.q: Can the judge reopen the proceedings?
o: No, because the case is already submitted
Yes, before finality to avoid injustice
Only upon the public prosecutor's motion
No, new witnesses wait for the appeal
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 24: at any time before finality of a judgment of conviction, the judge may motu proprio or on motion, with hearing, reopen the proceedings to avoid a miscarriage of justice (terminated within 30 days).
qs.key: Yes, before finality to avoid injustice
qs.lb: Rule 119, Sec. 24, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Cabarles v. Maceda (G.R. No. 161330, Feb. 20, 2007)

S.title: Judgment contents, promulgation, and new trial
S.base: Bea is tried for theft in an RTC in Cebu.

qs.q: The judge acquits Bea, writing only: "The accused is not guilty." Is the judgment complete?
o: Yes, an acquittal needs no explanation
No, it must state basis and civil finding
Yes, if the prosecutor raises no objection
No, it must also state the proper penalty
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 2: a judgment of acquittal must state whether the prosecution evidence absolutely failed or merely failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and determine whether the act or omission from which civil liability might arise did not exist.
qs.key: No, it must state basis and civil finding
qs.lb: Rule 120, Sec. 2, par. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Rewind: Bea is convicted. She is detained in a Davao jail.
o: The Cebu judge must travel to Davao
The Davao RTC executive judge on request
Any branch clerk of court in Davao City
No one until she is brought back to Cebu
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: when the accused is confined in another province or city, judgment may be promulgated by the executive judge of the RTC having jurisdiction over the place of confinement upon request of the trial court.
qs.key: The Davao RTC executive judge on request
qs.lb: Rule 120, Sec. 6, par. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Bea is in Cebu, but the judge is absent on the promulgation date.
o: Nobody; reset it
The clerk of court
The prosecutor
Bea's counsel
qs.ex: Under Rule 120, Sec. 6, par. 3, when the judge is absent or outside the province or city, the judgment may be promulgated by the clerk of court.
qs.key: The clerk of court
qs.lb: Rule 120, Sec. 6, par. 3, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Different case: Bea is convicted of a light offense. She is absent, but her counsel is present.
o: No, the accused must always be present
Yes, counsel or representative suffices
Only after an arrest warrant is served
Only if she submits written consent first
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: if the conviction is for a light offense, the judgment may be pronounced in the presence of the accused's counsel or representative.
qs.key: Yes, counsel or representative suffices
qs.lb: Rule 120, Sec. 6, par. 1, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Back to the theft conviction. Bea moves for new trial, offering a witness she knew about before trial but did not call.
o: Yes, any new witness justifies a new trial
No, it lacks reasonable diligence
Yes, provided the witness is credible
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 2(b): newly discovered evidence requires that it could not with reasonable diligence have been discovered and produced at the trial.
qs.key: No, it lacks reasonable diligence
qs.lb: Rule 121, Sec. 2(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Berry Rule (People v. Mariano, 1990); Custodio v. Sandiganbayan (G.R. Nos. 96027–28, 2005)

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted on truly newly discovered evidence.
qs.q: What happens to the evidence already presented?
o: All prior evidence is set aside
It stands; new evidence is added
Only the defense evidence stands
Only documentary evidence stands
qs.ex: Under Rule 121, Sec. 6(b) and (c), when a new trial is granted on the ground of newly discovered evidence, the evidence already adduced shall stand and the newly discovered and such other evidence as the court may allow shall be taken and considered together with it, while the original judgment is set aside or vacated.
qs.key: It stands; new evidence is added
qs.lb: Rule 121, Sec. 6(b) & (c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted because of an irregularity that prejudiced Bea at trial.
o: All previously adduced evidence stands
Affected proceedings are retaken anew
The criminal case is fully dismissed
The original judgment stays affirmed
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 6(a): when new trial is granted on errors of law or irregularities during trial, all proceedings and evidence affected thereby are set aside and taken anew; the original judgment is vacated.
qs.key: Affected proceedings are retaken anew
qs.lb: Rule 121, Sec. 6(a) & (c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: The judgment has become final. Bea now moves for new trial in the RTC.
o: Yes, a motion lies at any stage
No, it must precede final judgment
Yes, on newly discovered evidence
Only with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1: a motion for new trial or reconsideration must be filed at any time before a judgment of conviction becomes final.
qs.key: No, it must precede final judgment
qs.lb: Rule 121, Sec. 1, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

S.title: Appeal routes and higher courts
S.base: Cris is convicted in a criminal case.

qs.q: Cris was convicted by an MTC, which followed the same procedure as an RTC. Where and how does he appeal?
o: To the CA by petition for review
To the RTC by notice of appeal
To the SC by certiorari
To the RTC by petition for review
qs.ex: Rule 122, Secs. 2(a), 3(a). Rule 123: MTCs follow the same procedure as RTCs, except RTC-only provisions and cases under the 2022 Rules on Expedited Procedures (formerly summary procedure).
qs.key: To the RTC by notice of appeal
qs.lb: Rule 122, Secs. 2(a) & 3(a) & Rule 123, Sec. 1, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; A.M. No. 08-8-7-SC (2022 Rules on Expedited Procedures)

qs.tw: The RTC affirms on appeal. Cris wants to go to the CA.
o: Notice of appeal
Petition for review under Rule 42
Petition for certiorari under Rule 65
Automatic review
qs.ex: Under Rule 122, Sec. 3(b), an appeal to the Court of Appeals from a decision of the Regional Trial Court rendered in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction shall be by petition for review under Rule 42.
qs.key: Petition for review under Rule 42
qs.lb: Rule 122, Sec. 3(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Rule 42, Rules of Court

qs.tw: Different case: Cris was tried by the RTC and sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
o: Petition for review on certiorari to the SC
Notice of appeal to the CA
Automatic review by the SC
Petition for review to the CA
qs.ex: Under Rule 122, Sec. 3(c) and People v. Mateo (2004), an appeal from an RTC judgment imposing reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment is taken to the Court of Appeals by filing a notice of appeal with the RTC.
qs.key: Notice of appeal to the CA
qs.lb: Rule 122, Sec. 3(c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; People v. Mateo (G.R. Nos. 147678–87, July 7, 2004, En Banc); A.M. No. 00-5-03-SC

qs.tw: The CA affirms reclusion perpetua.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Petition for review on certiorari
Notice of appeal filed with the CA
Automatic review
Motion for reconsideration only
qs.ex: Under Rule 124, Sec. 13(c), when the Court of Appeals imposes reclusion perpetua, life imprisonment, or a lesser penalty, it renders and enters judgment, and an appeal from a CA judgment imposing reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment is taken to the Supreme Court by notice of appeal filed with the Court of Appeals.
qs.key: Notice of appeal filed with the CA
qs.lb: Rule 124, Sec. 13(c), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; A.M. No. 00-5-03-SC

qs.tw: Instead, the CA affirms a 10-year sentence.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Ordinary notice of appeal filed with the CA
Petition for review on certiorari (Rule 45)
Mandatory automatic review by the SC
Petition for review under Rule 42
qs.ex: Under Rule 122, Sec. 3(e) and Rule 125, Sec. 2, except in cases where the CA imposes reclusion perpetua, life imprisonment, or death, appeals to the Supreme Court from the Court of Appeals are taken by petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 on questions of law.
qs.key: Petition for review on certiorari (Rule 45)
qs.lb: Rule 122, Sec. 3(e) & Rule 125, Sec. 2, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Rule 45, Rules of Court

qs.tw: At the CA, Cris's counsel de oficio fails to file the appellant's brief on time.
qs.q: Can the CA dismiss the appeal for this?
o: Yes, failure to file a brief is always fatal
No, counsel de oficio is an exception
Yes, once thirty days have elapsed
Only if the Solicitor General moves
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 8: the CA may not dismiss an appeal for failure to file the appellant's brief when the appellant is represented by counsel de oficio.
qs.key: No, counsel de oficio is an exception
qs.lb: Rule 124, Sec. 8, par. 1, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Back at the trial court, Cris filed a notice of appeal but now wants to withdraw it. The records have not yet been forwarded.
o: No, an appeal can never be withdrawn
Yes, the trial court may allow withdrawal
Only with the Court of Appeals' prior approval
Only if the prosecution expressly agrees
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 12: before the record is forwarded to the appellate court, the trial court may allow the appellant to withdraw his appeal, rendering the judgment final.
qs.key: Yes, the trial court may allow withdrawal
qs.lb: Rule 122, Sec. 12, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: The offended party appeals only the amount of civil damages.
qs.q: Does this affect Cris's criminal conviction?
o: Yes, the entire criminal case reopens too
No, it does not affect the criminal aspect
Yes, the criminal penalty may be increased
Only if Cris also files his own appeal
qs.ex: Under Rule 122, Sec. 11(b), an appeal taken by the offended party from the civil aspect shall not affect the criminal aspect of the judgment or order appealed from.
qs.key: No, it does not affect the criminal aspect
qs.lb: Rule 122, Sec. 11(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Villareal v. Aliga (2014)

qs.tw: While the appeal is pending at the CA, Cris discovers new evidence material to his defense.
o: Nothing; simply await the CA decision
Move for new trial before CA finality
File a separate new case in the RTC
Elevate the evidence directly to the SC
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 14: at any time after appeal is perfected and before the CA judgment becomes final, the appellant may move for a new trial in the CA on the ground of newly discovered evidence.
qs.key: Move for new trial before CA finality
qs.lb: Rule 124, Sec. 14, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: The case reaches the SC en banc. The Justices are equally divided on acquittal, and re-deliberation does not break the tie.
o: The judgment of conviction is affirmed
Conviction reversed and Cris acquitted
The case is remanded for a new trial
The Chief Justice casts a deciding vote
qs.ex: Under Rule 125, Sec. 3, when the Supreme Court en banc is equally divided in opinion or the necessary majority cannot be had on whether to acquit the appellant, the case shall again be deliberated upon, and if no decision is reached after re-deliberation, the judgment of conviction of the lower court shall be reversed and the accused acquitted.
qs.key: Conviction reversed and Cris acquitted
qs.lb: Rule 125, Sec. 3, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Art. VIII, Sec. 4(2), 1987 Constitution

S.title: Getting and serving a search warrant
S.base: Police want a search warrant for Dina's house in Pasig for illegal firearms. No criminal case has been filed.

o: Any trial court anywhere in the country
Court with venue, or region for good cause
Only directly before the Supreme Court
Only the court of the police station's venue
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 2: apply in any court within whose territorial jurisdiction the crime was committed; or, for compelling reasons stated in the application, any court within the judicial region where the crime was committed or where the warrant shall be enforced.
qs.key: Court with venue, or region for good cause
qs.lb: Rule 126, Sec. 2(a)–(b), Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; A.M. No. 99-20-09-SC; Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp. v. Romars International Gases Corp. (G.R. No. 189669, 2015)

qs.tw: A criminal case for the same offense is already pending in a Pasig RTC branch.
o: Any regional trial court in Pasig City
Only the court hearing the pending case
Any court within the same judicial region
Strictly before the executive judge
qs.ex: Under Rule 126, Sec. 2, last paragraph, if the criminal action has already been filed, the application for a search warrant shall only be made in the court where the criminal action is pending.
qs.key: Only the court hearing the pending case
qs.lb: Rule 126, Sec. 2, last par., Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: The judge issues the warrant after reading only the applicant's affidavit, without asking any questions.
o: Yes, because the affidavit is under oath
No, judge must personally ask questions
Yes, provided the affidavit is detailed
Only if the public prosecutor signed it
qs.ex: Rule 126, Secs. 4–5: the judge must personally examine the complainant and witnesses in the form of searching questions and answers, in writing and under oath.
qs.key: No, judge must personally ask questions
qs.lb: Art. III, Sec. 2, 1987 Constitution; Rule 126, Secs. 4–5, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure; Bache & Co. (Phil.), Inc. v. Ruiz (G.R. No. L-32409, 1971); Silva v. Presiding Judge (G.R. No. 81756, 1991)

qs.tw: The warrant says nothing about the time of service. Police search at 11 p.m.
o: Yes, warrants may be served anytime
No, daytime applies unless directed
Yes, if the lawful occupant is awake
Only if executed on a weekend night
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 9: a search warrant must be served in the daytime, unless the affidavit asserts the property is on the person or in the place ordered searched and the warrant expressly directs service at any time.
qs.key: No, daytime applies unless directed
qs.lb: Rule 126, Sec. 9, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure

qs.tw: Police seize the guns. Dina is present, but they leave no receipt.

N: Imposable imprisonment threshold dividing exclusive original criminal jurisdiction between First-Level Courts (MTC/MeTC/MTCC/MCTC) and Regional Trial Courts (RTC)
Offenses punishable by imprisonment not exceeding 6 years fall under First-Level Courts; offenses punishable by more than 6 years fall under the RTC, regardless of the fine or accessory penalties.
Minimum salary grade threshold for public officers to fall under the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Sandiganbayan for offenses committed in relation to office
Certain enumerated officials (e.g., provincial governors, city mayors, city/provincial prosecutors, PNP provincial directors) fall under Sandiganbayan jurisdiction regardless of Salary Grade.

Monetary threshold of government damage or bribe separating Sandiganbayan from RTC original jurisdiction (for SG 27+ officials), and principal tax/fees threshold for Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) exclusive original criminal jurisdiction

In graft/bribery cases where the official is SG 27+, government damage or bribe must exceed ₱1,000,000.00 for Sandiganbayan original jurisdiction (if ≤ ₱1,000,000.00 or unspecified, RTC has original jurisdiction and Sandiganbayan has appellate jurisdiction). For criminal tax/customs violations, principal taxes/fees claimed must be ≥ ₱1,000,000.00 for CTA exclusive original jurisdiction.
Prosecutor filing (filing the complaint before the Office of the City or Provincial Prosecutor)
Act that interrupts the prescriptive period for RPC felonies and special penal laws (General Tolling Rule)
110, Sec. 1; People v. Consebido (En Banc, April 2, 2025)

Prescription begins to run from the day of commission, or from discovery by the offended party, authorities, or their agents if concealed (Blameless Ignorance Doctrine, Art. 91, RPC / Sec. 2, Act No. 3326). Filing the complaint for preliminary investigation with the prosecutor tolls prescription for both RPC crimes and special penal laws.
Direct court filing only (filing the Complaint or Information directly in court)
Exclusive act that interrupts the prescriptive period for violations of City or Municipal Ordinances (Exception to the General Tolling Rule)
110; Act No. 3326; Zaldivia v. Reyes; Jadewell v. Lidua
Filing a complaint with the Prosecutor’s Office does NOT toll ordinance prescription; only judicial proceedings filed directly in court interrupt the 2-month prescriptive period.
Prescriptive period for RPC crimes punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or reclusion temporal
Prescription starts from the day of commission, or from discovery under the Blameless Ignorance / Discovery Doctrine (Republic v. Desierto) if concealed.
Prescriptive period for Treason penalized under Act No. 3326
Applies to treason penalized under special penal law provisions.
Prescriptive period for RPC crimes punishable by other afflictive penalties (prision mayor, perpetual or temporary disqualification)
Prescriptive period for Cyberlibel under R.A. 10175 in relation to Article 90 of the RPC, counted from discovery
Resolves prior confusion—because Cyberlibel carries a penalty one degree higher than traditional RPC libel (making it an afflictive penalty), its prescriptive period is 15 years instead of 1 year.
Prescriptive period for special penal law offenses punishable by imprisonment for 6 years or more
Under People v. Consebido (En Banc, April 2, 2025), filing a complaint with the Prosecutor’s Office interrupts this period.
Prescriptive period for RPC crimes punishable by correctional penalties (prision correccional, suspension, destierro), except arresto mayor and libel
Prescriptive period for special penal law offenses punishable by imprisonment for 2 years or more but less than 6 years
Prescriptive period for RPC crimes punishable by arresto mayor
Prescriptive period for special penal law offenses punishable by imprisonment for more than 1 month but less than 2 years, including B.P. Blg. 22 (Bouncing Checks Law)

For B.P. Blg. 22, the 4-year period is counted from the lapse of 5 banking days from the drawer’s receipt of written notice of dishonor, and is interrupted by filing the complaint with the prosecutor (People v. Consebido).
Prescriptive period for traditional Libel and other similar offenses under Article 90 of the RPC
Prescriptive period for special penal law offenses punishable only by a fine or by imprisonment for not more than 1 month, or both
Prescriptive period for Oral Defamation (Slander) and Slander by Deed under Article 90 of the RPC
Prescriptive period for Light Offenses under Article 90 of the RPC
Under jurisprudence (Yapdiangco v. Buencamino), the 2-month prescriptive period for light offenses is computed as 60 days.
Prescriptive period for violations of City or Municipal Ordinances under Act No. 3326

Crucial Exception! Unlike other offenses, filing with the Prosecutor’s Office does NOT toll this period. It is interrupted only by filing the Information or Complaint directly in COURT (Zaldivia v. Reyes; Jadewell v. Lidua).
Before plea (as a matter of right, without leave of court)
Procedural stage at which both formal and substantial amendments to the Complaint or Information may generally be made without leave of court

Exception before plea: Any amendment that downgrades the nature of the offense charged or excludes any accused from the Complaint or Information requires a motion by the prosecutor, notice to the offended party, and leave of court.
After plea (formal amendments only with leave of court and no prejudice; substantial prohibited)

Procedural stage during which substantial amendments to the Information are strictly prohibited, and only formal amendments are permitted with leave of court and if it causes no prejudice to the rights of the accused
Exclusive procedural window for the private offended party to make a timely reservation of the right to institute a separate civil action
Reservation is prohibited in B.P. 22 cases (civil action for face value is mandatorily instituted with the criminal case).
Arts. 32, 33, 34 & 2176, Civil Code (independent civil actions survive against the estate)
Sources of civil obligation that survive against the estate or legal representative of the accused when death after arraignment or pending appeal extinguishes criminal and civil liability ex delicto

If the accused dies before final judgment, criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto (solely based on the crime under Art. 100, RPC) are extinguished, but independent civil actions predicated on law, contracts, quasi-contracts, and quasi-delicts (Arts. 32, 33, 34, and 2176) survive against the estate.
Maximum custodial detention period without judicial filing (delivery to judicial authorities) for warrantless arrests involving offenses punishable by light penalties or their equivalent

Counted by the hour from the start of detention (weekends and holidays do not stop the clock). Failure to file an Information or release the suspect within this window makes the arresting officers liable for Arbitrary Detention under Art. 125, RPC.
Maximum custodial detention period without judicial filing (delivery to judicial authorities) for warrantless arrests involving offenses punishable by correctional penalties or their equivalent

Maximum custodial detention period without judicial filing (delivery to judicial authorities) for warrantless arrests involving offenses punishable by afflictive or capital penalties, or their equivalent
Maximum custodial detention period without judicial charge (and maximum additional extension) for suspects arrested under Section 29 of R.A. 11479 (Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020)
Requires written authorization from the Anti-Terrorism Council (ATC) and immediate written notification to the nearest judge.
Maximum period from inception within which a regular preliminary investigation must be terminated if an arrested person signs an Article 125 waiver in writing and with assistance of counsel
The waiver is void unless executed in writing and signed by the detained person in the presence and with the assistance of independent counsel.
Period counted from learning of the filing of an inquest Information in court within which an accused arrested without a warrant may ask for a preliminary investigation
Exceeding 6 years (6 years & 1 day or more)
Imposable penalty threshold requiring a mandatory full Preliminary Investigation under DOJ Department Circular No. 15
The old 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day threshold is superseded; the quantum of proof is now Prima Facie Case with Reasonable Certainty of Conviction (PFC+RCC).
Imposable penalty range threshold for Expedited Preliminary Investigation (EPI) under DOJ Department Circular No. 28
Imposable penalty range threshold for Summary Investigation (SI) by the prosecutor under DOJ Department Circular No. 28
Period counted from the filing of the complaint within which the investigating prosecutor must either dismiss the complaint outright (if no ground to continue) or issue a subpoena to the respondent
Period counted from receipt of the subpoena and complaint within which the respondent must submit Counter-Affidavits and supporting documents
Motions to dismiss are strictly prohibited; if filed, they are treated as the counter-affidavit itself.
Maximum allowable extension period granted to a respondent to file a Counter-Affidavit, allowed only once and strictly in the interest of justice
Period counted from the date of resolution within which the investigating prosecutor must forward the record of the case to the Provincial or City Prosecutor, Chief State Prosecutor, or Ombudsman
Period counted from receipt of the investigating prosecutor’s resolution within which the Provincial or City Prosecutor, Chief State Prosecutor, or Ombudsman must act on the resolution
Period counted from the filing of the Information within which the judge must personally evaluate the resolution and evidence to dismiss the case or issue a warrant of arrest or commitment order
A Commitment Order is issued if the accused is already in custody (e.g., inquest); a Warrant of Arrest is issued if the accused is still at large.
Period counted from the court’s order within which the prosecutor must submit additional evidence if the judge is in doubt regarding probable cause
Maximum total period counted from the filing of the Information within which the trial judge must resolve the existence of probable cause when additional evidence was ordered
Period counted from receipt of the warrant of arrest within which the head of the executing office must cause the warrant to be executed
An arrest warrant does NOT expire after 10 days; unlike a search warrant, it remains enforceable indefinitely until served or lifted.
Period counted after the expiration of the execution period within which the executing officer must make a formal return/report to the issuing judge if the arrest warrant is executed or unexecuted
Matter of right (before/after MTC conviction; before RTC conviction of non-capital offense)

Legal nature of bail (a) before or after conviction by First-Level Courts (MTC/MeTC/MTCC/MCTC), and (b) before conviction by the RTC of an offense not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment
Matter of discretion (after RTC conviction of non-capital offense)
Legal nature of bail upon conviction by the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of an offense not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment
Imposable penalty threshold upon RTC conviction where bail pending appeal becomes discretionary and must be denied or cancelled if any of the 5 bail-negating circumstances are present

The 5 bail-negating circumstances: (1) Recidivism/habituality; (2) Escape or bail jump; (3) Offense committed while on probation, parole, or conditional pardon; (4) Probability of flight; (5) Undue risk of committing another offense during appeal.
Standard bail reduction percentage recommended for qualified indigent litigants under DOJ Department Circular No. 11 (2023)
Helps prevent excessive bail and decongest detention facilities for impoverished accused.
Period counted from the approval of a property bond within which the accused must cause the annotation of the lien on the certificate of title or tax declaration and report compliance to the court
Maximum period of preventive imprisonment after which a person detained for an offense punishable only by destierro must be released

Period counted from the order of forfeiture of bail within which the bondsmen must produce the body of their principal (the accused) and show cause why judgment should not be rendered against them for the amount of the bail
Distance of a defense witness’s residence from the place of trial that justifies their conditional examination before trial
General period within which the court must arraign the accused (if not preventively detained), counted from the date the court acquires jurisdiction over the person of the accused
Period counted from the filing of the Information against a preventively detained accused within which the case must be raffled and the records transmitted to the judge to whom the case was raffled
Shortened period within which the court must arraign the accused if preventively detained, counted from the clerk’s receipt of the raffled case records
Minimum period granted to the accused after entering a plea of not guilty to prepare for trial

Maximum allowable period of suspension of arraignment due to a pending Petition for Review with the DOJ or the Office of the President, counted from the filing of the petition with the reviewing office
After this period expires, arraignment must proceed even if the DOJ or Office of the President has not yet resolved the petition.
Before plea (before entering a plea at arraignment)
General procedural cutoff for the accused to file a Motion to Quash the Complaint or Information, after which waivable grounds are deemed waived under the Omnibus Motion Rule

Time-bar period counted from issuance of the order of provisional dismissal after which the dismissal becomes permanent without revival, for offenses punishable by imprisonment not exceeding 6 years or a fine of any amount
Requires express consent of the accused and notice to the offended party.
Time-bar period counted from issuance of the order of provisional dismissal after which the dismissal becomes permanent without revival, for offenses punishable by imprisonment of more than 6 years
Number of specific grounds of a Motion to Quash that are not waived even if raised after plea (may be raised at any stage of the proceedings)

The 4 non-waivable grounds: (1) The facts charged do not constitute an offense; (2) Lack of jurisdiction over the offense charged; (3) Extinction of the offense or criminal liability; (4) Double jeopardy.
General period within which pre-trial must be held (if the accused is not preventively detained), counted after the court acquires jurisdiction over the person of the accused
Shortened period within which pre-trial must be held if the accused is under preventive detention
Period counted after the termination of the pre-trial conference within which the trial judge must issue the Pre-Trial Order
Admissions made during pre-trial cannot be used against the accused unless reduced to writing and signed by both the accused and defense counsel (Rule 118, Sec. 2).
Both accused & counsel (in writing and signed by both)
Mandatory formal requirement for all agreements or admissions made or entered during the pre-trial conference to be admissible in evidence against the accused

Maximum imposable penalty threshold (imprisonment or fine) under the Katarungang Pambarangay Law for offenses between neighbors in the same city or municipality requiring mandatory prior barangay conciliation
Offenses punishable by 1 year or less or a fine of ₱5,000.00 or less between neighbors in the same city/municipality require prior Lupon conciliation as a condition precedent.
Minimum preparation time for the accused after plea before trial starts
Maximum period within which trial must commence, counted from receipt of the Pre-Trial Order
Maximum excluded delay resulting from pre-trial proceedings in computing speedy trial time limits
Maximum total duration of a regular trial, counted from the first day of trial
Maximum total duration of trial conducted via the Judicial Affidavit Rule
Period counted from notice of the order granting a new trial within which the new trial must commence
Non-extendible period counted after the prosecution rests its case for the accused to file a Motion for Leave of Court to file Demurrer to Evidence
Non-extendible period counted from receipt of the motion for leave for the prosecution to comment on or oppose the Motion for Leave to file Demurrer to Evidence
Non-extendible period counted from notice of the order granting leave of court for the accused to file the actual Demurrer to Evidence
Non-extendible period counted from receipt of the demurrer for the prosecution to file its opposition to the Demurrer to Evidence
Period within which the trial court must resolve the Demurrer to Evidence

The Demurrer Trap: If filed with leave and denied, the accused may present defense evidence; if filed without leave and denied, the accused unconditionally waives the right to present evidence and submits the case for judgment (GMA v. People). Granting a demurrer equals an acquittal, which immediately triggers double jeopardy.

Period counted from the order granting a motion to reopen the case (filed before finality of judgment of conviction to avoid a miscarriage of justice) within which the reopened proceedings must be terminated
Number of strict statutory conditions required under Rule 119, Section 17 to discharge an accused to be utilized as a State Witness

The 5 requisites: (1) Absolute necessity for the testimony of the accused whose discharge is requested; (2) No other direct evidence available for the proper prosecution of the offense committed, except his testimony; (3) Testimony can be substantially corroborated in its material points; (4) Said accused does not appear to be the most guilty; and (5) Said accused has not at any time been convicted of any offense involving moral turpitude.
Period counted from promulgation of judgment after which a judgment of conviction becomes final and executory (absent a timely appeal, MNT/MR, probation application, waiver, or service of sentence)

Period counted from promulgation/recording in the criminal docket within which an accused convicted in absentia must surrender and file a motion for leave of court to regain statutory remedies against the judgment
If the accused fails to surrender within this window without justifiable cause, they permanently lose their right to avail of post-judgment remedies.
Period counted from notice/promulgation of judgment (within the period for perfecting an appeal) within which an accused may apply for probation
Applying for probation waives the right to appeal.

Special window counted from notice/promulgation of the modified appellate judgment allowing an accused to apply for probation if an appellate court modifies a non-probationable sentence into a probationable penalty
Imposable imprisonment penalty threshold that disqualifies an offender from probation under P.D. 968 / R.A. 10707
Period counted from promulgation of a judgment of conviction (before it becomes final) within which the accused must file a Motion for New Trial or Motion for Reconsideration
Exclusively available to the accused; the prosecution cannot move for reconsideration or new trial from an acquittal due to double jeopardy.
New period to file an appeal granted under the Neypes / Judith Yu v. Samson-Tatad rule, counted from receipt of the order denying a timely Motion for New Trial or Motion for Reconsideration
Pro forma motions do not toll the period and do not generate a fresh period.

Standard reglementary period counted from promulgation or notice of judgment (or from notice of denial of MNT/MR) to file a Notice of Appeal (MTC to RTC under Rule 40; RTC original to CA under Rule 41)
Reglementary period counted from notice of the decision (or denial of MNT/MR) to file a Petition for Review from the RTC’s appellate decision to the Court of Appeals (Rule 42)
Initial extension period grantable by the Court of Appeals under Rule 42 upon proper motion and payment of docket fees before expiration of the reglementary period
Further extendible only for the most compelling reason by a maximum of another 15 days (30 days maximum total extension).
Reglementary period counted from notice of judgment or final order (or denial of MNT/MR) to file an Appeal by Certiorari on pure questions of law with the Supreme Court (Rule 45)
Maximum extension period granted by the Supreme Court for justifiable reasons upon motion and payment of fees for filing a Rule 45 petition
Period counted after perfection of the appeal within which the Clerk of Court of the trial court must transmit the complete records and TSNs to the appellate court
Period counted from receipt of notice from the RTC clerk of court for the appellant to submit an Appeal Memorandum to the RTC under Rule 122, Section 9
Period counted from receipt of the appellant’s memorandum (or expiration of the period to file it) for the appellee to submit a Counter-Memorandum to the RTC under Rule 122, Section 9
Failure to file an appeal memorandum in a criminal case is NOT a ground for dismissal (Sanico v. People), unlike in civil cases under Rule 40; the RTC must decide based on the record.

Period counted from notice of the CA’s resolution under People v. Olpindo (En Banc, 2022) for an accused to file a manifestation adopting an erroneous motu proprio elevation as a timely Notice of Appeal
Maximum imposable criminal penalty threshold (imprisonment or fine) for general criminal offenses to be covered under Summary Procedure in First-Level Courts
Maximum imposable fine limit for damage to property through criminal negligence under Article 365 of the RPC to be covered by Summary Procedure
Period counted from receipt of summons under the Rules on Summary Procedure for the defendant to file counter-affidavits and judicial affidavits
General rule: No warrant of arrest is issued; only summons. Warrants issue only if the accused fails to appear after summons, jumps bail, or is under lawful inquest.
Period counted following receipt of the affidavits under the Rules on Summary Procedure within which the preliminary conference must be held
Period counted following the termination of the preliminary conference (or trial) under the Rules on Summary Procedure within which the first-level court must render judgment
The RTC decision on appeal in cases under Summary/Expedited Procedure is final, executory, and unappealable (Sec. 21, Summary Rules).
Reglementary period counted from notice of judgment to appeal from the Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court via Notice of Appeal when the penalty imposed is reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment
Quorum of a regular Division in the Court of Appeals, and the unanimous vote required for a Division to pronounce a judgment
Composition of the Special Division of the Court of Appeals convened when unanimity in a regular Division is not reached
A majority vote of 3 Justices in the Special Division of 5 is needed to decide the case.
Period counted from receipt of notice from the CA clerk that the records are complete within which the appellant must file the Appellant’s Brief in the Court of Appeals
Period counted from receipt of the Appellant’s Brief within which the appellee must file the Appellee’s Brief in the Court of Appeals
Period counted from receipt of the Appellee’s Brief within which the appellant may file a Reply Brief in the Court of Appeals
Maximum cumulative extension of time permitted for filing briefs in the Court of Appeals
Period counted from notice of the decision or final resolution within which to file a Motion for Reconsideration in the Court of Appeals
Total constitutional membership of the Supreme Court (1 Chief Justice and 14 Associate Justices)
Number of operating divisions of the Supreme Court when sitting in Divisions
Each Supreme Court Division consists of 5 Justices.
Quorum of a Supreme Court Division, and the minimum number of concurring votes required in a Division to pronounce a judgment
Quorum required for Supreme Court En Banc sessions

Mandatory Acquittal Rule: If the Supreme Court En Banc is equally divided in opinion (a tie vote) after re-deliberation, the conviction is reversed and the accused is acquitted based on the presumption of innocence and the equipoise doctrine.
Number of mandatory constitutional and statutory requisites that must concur for the issuance of a valid search warrant

The 4 requisites: (1) Probable cause in connection with one specific offense; (2) Personally determined by the judge; (3) After examination under oath or affirmation, in searching questions and answers, of the complainant and witnesses; (4) Particularly describing the place to be searched and the things to be seized.
Statutory period of validity of a search warrant counted from its date of issuance
On the 11th day, it becomes functus officio and void; any search conducted after 10 days is illegal.
Presumptive period of the day during which a search warrant must be served, unless expressly authorized in the warrant for a nighttime search

Nighttime searches are strictly prohibited unless the affidavit positively asserts that the property is on the person or in the place ordered to be searched, and the judge inserts an express direction for a nighttime search in the warrant.

Number of witnesses of sufficient age and discretion residing in the same locality required to be present during a search of a house, room, or premises when the lawful occupant and members of their family are absent

Two-Witness Rule: No search of a house, room, or any other premises shall be made except in the presence of the lawful occupant thereof or any member of his family or, in the absence of the latter, two witnesses of sufficient age and discretion residing in the same locality.
Rule of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure that governs the standards, grounds, and procedure for preliminary attachment as a provisional remedy in criminal cases
Available only when the civil action has not been waived, reserved, or independently instituted, and one of the grounds under Rule 127, Sec. 2 is present.
At least 2 devices (1 BWC + 1 ARD, or ≥ 2 ARDs)
Mandatory minimum number and combination of recording devices required to be worn and activated by executing officers during the service of an arrest or search warrant
Mandatory judicial prerequisite before law enforcement officers may use Alternative Recording Devices (ARDs) when Body-Worn Cameras are unavailable during warrant execution

Crucial Rule! Officers cannot unilaterally decide to use ARDs. For Arrest Warrants, they must file an ex parte motion showing justifiable grounds. For Search Warrants, the request must be expressly stated in the application. If a BWC unexpectedly malfunctions during execution, ARDs may be used immediately, provided an explanatory affidavit under oath is submitted with the return.
Minimum video resolution required for an Alternative Recording Device (ARD) under the BWC Rules
Minimum standard video frame rate required for an Alternative Recording Device (ARD) under the BWC Rules
Minimum continuous battery life required for an Alternative Recording Device (ARD) under the BWC Rules
Minimum continuous audio-video storage capacity required for an Alternative Recording Device (ARD) under the BWC Rules
Period counted from the time of capture within which recorded BWC/ARD data must be downloaded by the designated Data Custodian to an external media storage device
Period counted from data downloading within which authorized persons (subject, counsel, spouse, or next of kin) may review and obtain a copy of the BWC/ARD recording, provided consent is given
Maximum period an executing officer may retain a backup copy of BWC/ARD recordings when allowed with leave of court
Period under the BWC Rules within which the executing officer must file a report with the judge stating the reasons why an arrest warrant remained unexecuted
Minimum period counted from the date of the transaction that service providers must preserve traffic data and subscriber information
Minimum period counted from receipt of a preservation order from law enforcement that service providers must preserve content data
Maximum extension period that law enforcement authorities may order for the preservation of computer data
Maximum initial validity period of any cybercrime warrant (WSSECD, WDCD, WICD, WECD) counted from its date of issuance
Maximum one-time extension period grantable by the issuing cybercrime court for the validity of a cybercrime warrant upon motion for justifiable reasons
Period counted from receipt of a Warrant to Disclose Computer Data (WDCD) within which a service provider or person must disclose or submit the required computer data
Period counted from implementation or expiration of a Warrant to Disclose Computer Data (WDCD) within which law enforcement must submit a return to the issuing court
Period counted from implementation of a WSSECD or WECD within which law enforcement must file an Initial Return with the issuing cybercrime court
Period counted from implementation of a WSSECD or WECD within which law enforcement must file a Final Return with the issuing cybercrime court
Period counted after a criminal action is instituted within which a motion must be filed for the deposit or custody of seized computer data with the trial court
Period counted from filing within which the court must act on a motion for custody or deposit of seized digital data
Time window after deposit of seized digital data after which stored digital data must be returned or destroyed if no formal criminal case has been instituted
Mandatory physical destruction standard (number of holes drilled completely through magnetic hard drive platters) when the court orders destruction of seized computer data
Number of special regional hub cities whose designated Cybercrime Courts possess authority to issue cybercrime warrants enforceable nationwide and outside Philippine territory
The 8 regional hub cities: Quezon City, Manila, Makati City, Pasig City, Cebu City, Iloilo City, Davao City, and Cagayan de Oro City.
